claims.text: The large, sharp, and hysteretic magnetocaloric response in non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type HEAs is governed by an interplay between residual stress, microstructural inhomogeneity, and strong magnetoelastic coupling.
The relevant magnetocaloric response occurs through a first-order magnetostructural transition.
Controlled low-temperature post-deposition annealing will reduce residual stress in FeMnNiGeSi-type films.
Reducing residual stress will make the transition smoother and reduce hysteretic losses during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
As-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type films have an ordered, single-phase hexagonal structure.
As-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type films contain inherent residual stress.
As-deposited films contain microstructural features such as nano-twins and domain boundaries.
Annealing below the precipitation or phase-change threshold can relax residual stress without altering the principal hexagonal phase.
Residual-stress magnitude and distribution, nano-twins, and sub-grain boundaries mediate magnetoelastic coupling during the transition.
Annealing reduces local lattice distortion and inhomogeneous strain.
Reduced lattice distortion and inhomogeneous strain lower the energy barrier for the magnetostructural transition.
Lowering the transition barrier produces a broader and less abrupt entropy change.
Lowering the transition barrier diminishes hysteresis during magnetic-field cycling.
Annealed samples will have a lower magnetic-field threshold for initiating the transition than as-deposited samples.
Annealing will make the magnetocaloric effect more reversible than in the as-deposited baseline.
As-deposited films exhibit a sharp, first-order transition with a large but hysteretic entropy change under low-field cooling cycles.
The predicted effects should hold only near the magnetostructural-transition temperature, under low applied fields, and when annealing causes neither precipitation nor another phase change.
Compositional disorder may also influence magnetoelastic coupling.
